Every analysis in this guide goes through the same steps. A **question** ("does
smoking cause coronary heart disease, and by how much?") becomes an
**estimand**: a precise quantity, such as the risk ratio of a 10-year coronary
event for smokers against non-smokers with the same age and sex. A **design**
gathers data that can estimate it. A **causal diagram** says which variables to
adjust for. A **model** turns the data into a number, and the number is
**interpreted** on the scale of the estimand. This page covers the last two
steps: the measures epidemiology uses and how the coefficients of its models
are read. The next pages cover the designs, the diagrams and mediation
[@rothman2021; @hernan2020].

::: {#fig-strategy}
```{r}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 1.6
boxes <- data.frame(id = c("q", "e", "d", "g", "a", "m", "i"), x = (0:6) * 2.55, y = 0,
                    label = c("Question", "Estimand", "Design", "DAG", "Adjustment\nset", "Model", "Interpretation"),
                    role = c("other", "exposure", "other", "confounder", "confounder", "mediator", "outcome"))
links <- data.frame(from = boxes$id[-7], to = boxes$id[-1])
both(flow_fig, boxes, links, w = 2.0, h = 0.9)
```
From the question to its answer. Each page of this guide covers some of these steps.
:::

## Measures of frequency

| measure | definition | example | typical design |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Prevalence** | proportion of a population that has the condition at a time | 18% of adults have hypertension | cross-sectional |
| **Risk** (cumulative incidence) | proportion of people free of the outcome at the start who develop it over a period | 8% have a coronary event in 10 years | cohort, trial |
| **Rate** (incidence density) | new cases per unit of person-time | 2.5 breast cancers per 1000 woman-years | cohort |
| **Odds** | probability / (1 − probability) | a risk of 0.2 is odds of 0.25 | case-control (only odds ratios) |
| **Hazard** | instantaneous rate among those still at risk at a given time | | cohort with times (Cox) |

Prevalence mixes how often a condition starts and how long it lasts: in a
steady population, **prevalence ≈ incidence rate × mean duration**. A
treatment that keeps patients alive longer *raises* prevalence. A risk always
refers to a period ("10-year risk"), and it requires everyone to be followed
for that period or a method that handles censoring (Kaplan-Meier). When another
event can prevent the outcome (death from other causes before a cancer
relapse), the risk of the outcome is a **cumulative incidence** in the presence
of a **competing event**. One minus Kaplan-Meier, which censors the competing
deaths, overstates it.

## Measures of association

| measure | definition | estimated by |
|---|---|---|
| Risk difference (RD) | risk~1~ − risk~0~ | cohort, trial (2×2 table, binomial model with identity link) |
| Number needed to treat (NNT) | 1 / \|RD\| | trial |
| Risk ratio (RR) | risk~1~ / risk~0~ | cohort, trial, cross-sectional (prevalence ratio) |
| Rate ratio (IRR) | rate~1~ / rate~0~ | cohort (Poisson regression with log person-time as offset) |
| Hazard ratio (HR) | hazard~1~ / hazard~0~, assumed constant over time | cohort, trial (Cox regression) |
| Odds ratio (OR) | odds~1~ / odds~0~ | any design; the only one a case-control study gives |
| Mean difference | mean~1~ − mean~0~ | linear regression |
| Ratio of geometric means | exp(mean of log~1~ − mean of log~0~) | linear regression of a log outcome |

Difference measures say how many people are affected, and that is what
decisions need. Ratio measures say how strong the association is, and they are
usually more stable across populations with different baseline risks. Report
both when you can: a risk ratio of 2 means 10 extra cases per 1000 people if
the baseline risk is 1%, and 200 if it is 20%.

### The odds ratio is not a risk ratio

The odds ratio approaches the risk ratio only when the outcome is rare
(@fig-or-rr). A case-control study of a rare disease therefore estimates the
risk (or rate) ratio. A cross-sectional study of a common condition analysed
with logistic regression reports odds ratios that look much stronger than the
prevalence ratios.

::: {#fig-or-rr}
```{r}
#| renderings: [light, dark]
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.6
or_rr <- function(mode) {
    p <- PAL(mode)
    r0 <- seq(0.005, 0.45, length.out = 200)
    d <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1.5, 2, 3), function(rr) {
        r1 <- pmin(rr * r0, 0.999)
        data.frame(r0 = r0, or = (r1 / (1 - r1)) / (r0 / (1 - r0)), rr = factor(sprintf("RR = %s", rr), levels = sprintf("RR = %s", c(1.5, 2, 3))))
    }))
    ggplot(d, aes(r0, or, colour = rr)) + geom_hline(yintercept = c(1.5, 2, 3), colour = p$faint, linetype = "dashed") +
        geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + scale_colour_manual(values = unname(p$role[c("exposure", "mediator", "outcome")]), name = NULL) +
        scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(1, 12)) +
        labs(x = "risk in the unexposed", y = "odds ratio") + theme_plot(mode)
}
both(or_rr)
```
The odds ratio for a fixed risk ratio (dashed lines), by the risk in the unexposed: equal when the outcome is rare, ever larger as it becomes common.
:::

### Conditional and marginal: non-collapsibility

The odds ratio and the hazard ratio have a property that surprises many
people. Suppose a treatment multiplies the odds by 3 in every subgroup of
patients and the subgroups are perfectly balanced between the arms, so nothing
is confounded. The odds ratio of the whole trial is still *smaller* than 3
[@greenland1999b]. Risk differences and risk ratios do not behave this way.

```{r}
strata <- data.frame(group = c("low risk", "high risk"), r0 = c(0.10, 0.60))
odds <- function(r) r / (1 - r); risk <- function(o) o / (1 + o)
strata$r1 <- risk(3 * odds(strata$r0))
m0 <- mean(strata$r0); m1 <- mean(strata$r1)
tab <- rbind(strata, data.frame(group = "whole population (half each)", r0 = m0, r1 = m1))
tab$OR <- odds(tab$r1) / odds(tab$r0); tab$RR <- tab$r1 / tab$r0; tab$RD <- tab$r1 - tab$r0
knitr::kable(transform(tab, r0 = round(r0, 3), r1 = round(r1, 3), OR = round(OR, 2), RR = round(RR, 2), RD = round(RD, 3)),
             col.names = c("", "risk, control", "risk, treated", "OR", "RR", "RD"), row.names = FALSE)
```

Both subgroups have an odds ratio of 3, and the whole population has
`r round(odds(m1) / odds(m0), 2)`. Neither number is wrong: they answer
different questions. The **conditional** odds ratio is the effect for a patient
with given characteristics; the **marginal** one is the effect on the
population. In a trial the crude analysis estimates the marginal effect and an
analysis adjusted for prognostic variables the conditional one, which is
further from 1. studysim generates data with conditional effects, and its
answer key shows both for trials (*absolute effects in the trial*).

```{r}
trial_table("indomethacin_ercp", "pancreatitis")
```

## Models and how to read their coefficients

| outcome | model | exp(β) or β is | jamovi |
|---|---|---|---|
| continuous | linear regression | β: difference in the mean per unit of x | *Regression ▸ Linear Regression* |
| continuous, skewed | linear regression of log(y) | exp(β): ratio of geometric means | *Compute* log(y), then linear regression |
| binary | logistic regression | odds ratio | *Regression ▸ Logistic Regression ▸ 2 Outcomes* |
| binary, matched sets | conditional logistic regression | odds ratio within sets | **condLogReg** |
| count or rate | Poisson (negative binomial) regression, log person-time as offset | rate ratio | **GAMLj** |
| time to event | Cox regression | hazard ratio | **prognosis** |

The same rules apply to every model:

- **A coefficient is the effect of its variable with the other variables in the
  model held fixed.** It is a *conditional* effect. Whether it is the effect you
  want depends on which variables are in the model: the
  [causal diagram](guide-dags.qmd) decides that, not the model.
- **Per unit.** A coefficient for age is *per year*. A hazard ratio of 1.05 per
  year is 1.05^10^ = 1.63 per 10 years. Choose units that make sense: per 10
  mmHg, per 5 kg/m², per standard deviation.
- **Per level.** A categorical variable gets one coefficient per level, each
  against the reference level. Changing the reference changes the numbers but
  not the model.
- **Log scale.** Logistic, Poisson and Cox coefficients are logarithms: exp(β)
  is the ratio, and effects of several variables multiply. A log-transformed
  exposure gives the effect per doubling (log~2~) or per tenfold increase (log~10~).
- **Interaction.** With a product term X × Z, the coefficient of X is the effect
  of X *when Z is at its reference or zero*, and the interaction coefficient is
  how much that effect changes per unit of Z. If zero is not a meaningful value
  of Z (a BMI of zero), centre Z first, or the main effects become meaningless.
  This is the problem studysim's `center:` solves in its own scenarios.
- **The intercept** is the outcome (or its log odds or log rate) when every
  variable is at zero or its reference: rarely of interest, and meaningless
  without centring.
- **Categorising a continuous variable** loses information and leaves residual
  confounding within the categories. It is useful for showing a shape (dose
  response), not for adjustment.
- **Small numbers.** Logistic and Cox models need roughly ten events per
  parameter; with fewer, coefficients are unstable and biased away from the
  null [@peduzzi1996]. studysim warns when a study falls short.

### Effect modification and interaction

**Effect modification** means the effect of X differs between groups of Z: the
risk ratio of BMI for breast cancer is below 1 before menopause and above 1
after it. Whether it appears depends on the scale: effects that are constant on
the ratio scale differ on the difference scale whenever baseline risks differ,
and vice versa. Report the effect within each level of the modifier, on both
scales if possible. A modifier is not something to adjust away: it is a result.
A causal diagram shows which variables cause which, not how their effects
combine, so it cannot show effect modification.

### What studysim's answer key reports

| column | estimand |
|---|---|
| *Direct (conditional)* | the effect in the generating model, every other variable fixed |
| *Total* | the effect of changing the variable while its consequences change too, given the variables it does not cause ([Causal diagrams](guide-dags.qmd)) |
| *Crude* | the association without adjustment |
| *Adjusted (all)* | the conditional association given every measured variable |
| *Adjusted (DAG)* | the association given the measured variables that the diagram says to adjust for |
| *Absolute effects* (trials) | risks per arm, RD, NNT, marginal and conditional OR or HR |
